text: Handle electrostatic-sensitive components (e.g., holding a motherboard by the edges without touching pins).
Perform tight-space cable management (routing, zipping, and hiding cables behind a desk or PC chassis).
Administer pet medication (e.g., hiding a pill in a treat, dropping liquid into a water bowl).

Accessibility beyond mobility: describe layout and obstacles for low-vision residents, read mail and labels aloud, flash lights for the doorbell and alarms for deaf residents, keep furniture in consistent positions, dementia-friendly routines (labels, door checks).
Answer the doorbell or intercom; screen visitors and decline solicitors; let in expected guests; supervise repair people; accept and sign for deliveries.
Take and relay messages ("tell the kids dinner's ready"), announce visitors, set up and tidy for video calls, take group photos.
Hospitality: simple cocktails and mocktails, uncork wine, open cans and bottles, offer slippers, follow household rules on who may be served alcohol.

section: Reaching, climbing, and fixing. Tool handling stops at basic hand tools, and there's no height access.
text: Tools to add: drill/driver, stud finder, wall anchors, utility knife, scissors, staple gun, caulk gun, Allen keys.
Hazardous and bulky disposal: batteries, bulbs, e-waste, paint, aerosols, old medications, cooking oil, old furniture; stage items until drop-off day and transport them.

Away mode. Your departure routine covers daily exits. Add a vacation or house-sitting mode: arm the alarm, set lights on timers, bring in mail and packages, water plants, check for leaks and pests, run taps, check the freezer after an outage, care for pets, send status photos.
Diets and planning: halal, kosher, vegan, gluten-free, low-sodium, diabetic, texture-modified; meal planning; scaling recipes; baby food.

Vehicles, bikes, and errands (only if scope goes past the property line). Refuel, check and inflate tires, top off washer fluid, change wipers, jump-start, change a flat, scrape ice and snow, check the back seat before locking, check a car seat; lube a bike chain, patch a flat, charge an e-bike; curbside pickup, pharmacy, post office, donation and return drop-offs.

Situational variations. Apartments and condos (elevators, shared laundry, HOA rules), regional standards (metric vs. imperial, front vs. top-load, induction vs. gas, shoes-off homes), languages, accents, and speech differences, residents with disabilities or dementia, residents' emotional states, and robot-side degradation (dirty camera, low battery, network down, a failing arm).
intentionally left out, and where everything belongs.
“Put this somewhere safe.” “Safe” changes depending on whether the object is fragile, hot, valuable, dangerous to pets, sensitive to moisture, etc.
“Get this out of here.” It must determine whether that means trash it, relocate it, store it, return it, or simply move it to another room.
“Deal with this mess.” It has to inspect the situation and create its own cleanup plan.
“Make some room.” Requires rearranging objects without making the environment worse.
“Set this room up for a party.” Number of guests, seating, food locations, walking paths, decorations, trash locations, and breakable objects all matter.
“Make the house presentable before guests arrive.” It must prioritize visible problems rather than blindly deep-cleaning everything.
“Clean whatever needs cleaning.” Requires inspection, prioritization, and deciding when something is clean enough.
“Do a quick cleanup.” Requires balancing quality against time.
“Prepare everything I’ll need tomorrow.” Requires reasoning from calendar/context, weather, activities, school/work needs, and personal habits.
“Pack the fragile stuff carefully.” It has to recognize fragility and invent appropriate packing strategies.
“Make this fit in the box.” Requires spatial reasoning, rotation, rearrangement, folding, and possibly choosing another box.
“Load the car so the important things are easy to reach.” Requires understanding future use order.
“Put away the groceries properly.” It may encounter unfamiliar food and must infer pantry, refrigerator, freezer, or countertop storage.
“Reorganize this cabinet so everything fits better.” Requires 3D planning and category reasoning.
“Make more room in the refrigerator.” Requires rearranging containers while considering temperature zones, spills, expiration, and food safety.
“Use these leftovers before they go bad.” Requires inspecting ingredients, judging compatible combinations, and planning a meal.
“Make dinner with whatever we have.” One of the hardest: identify ingredients, possible dishes, missing substitutes, preparation order, and dietary constraints.
“Find something soft to protect this.” It must select padding from unrelated household items.
“Carry all of these in one trip if you can.” Requires deciding how objects can be stacked, held, bagged, or transported together.
“Move everything off this table except what we still need.” Requires understanding the current activity.
“Leave the important stuff.” Requires distinguishing importance contextually.
“Don’t move anything that looks intentional.” Requires interpreting arrangements rather than just object categories.
“The room feels weird. Check it.” Very ambiguous: temperature, smell, noise, lighting, objects out of place, or equipment malfunction.
“Make sure nothing looks wrong.” General anomaly detection across an open world.
“Find the thing I was using earlier.” Requires tracking recent human-object interactions.
“Find something my kid hid.” Requires adversarial search through plausible hiding locations.
“Find where the dog took my sock.” Requires reasoning about pet behavior.
“Put it where I usually put it.” Requires personalized long-term memory.
“Put everything back exactly how it was.” Requires high-fidelity spatial memory.
“Zip this bag even though it’s really full.” Requires rearranging contents and controlling deformation.
“This lid doesn’t fit. Find the right one.” Requires shape matching among similar objects.
“Bring in anything valuable.” Requires semantic judgment about value.
“Make a path through this clutter.” Requires choosing what can safely be moved and where.
“Open the door for the delivery person but keep the pets inside.” Multi-agent dynamic reasoning.
“Put this back together.” Requires remembering or inferring previous structure.
“Do this before it becomes a problem.” Requires predictive maintenance reasoning.
“Use your best judgment.” The robot has to choose without explicit procedural instruction.

“We’re out of paper towels; find something else to clean this up.” The robot must evaluate the nature of the spill (oil, water, biohazard) and find a suitable, safe alternative (a rag, a sponge, newspaper) without ruining a nice towel.
“Make a meal using only ingredients that expire this week.” Combines inventory scanning, expiration date reading, and recipe generation on the fly.
“Hide the presents where the kids won’t find them.” Requires keeping secrets, tracking who knows what, and modeling how kids search (the mirror image of your “find something my kid hid”).
“Why did you put it there?” Requires explaining its reasoning in a way the person can correct.
“Run the house while we’re away for a week.” Requires long-horizon autonomy, contingency handling, and knowing when to escalate.
“Figure out how this washer works.” Requires reading the panel and manual, then testing options safely.
“Learn the house.” Requires mapping rooms, objects, owners, no-go zones, shutoff locations, and the emergency plan, including in a home that isn’t yours.
“Get ready for the storm / the plumber / the newborn.” Requires building an event-specific prep list from context.
